items.title: Jam update: Sat 6:17 AM
items.content_html:
Jam update: Sat 6:17 AM

Saturday, November 14, 2026 at 6:17 AM Central

Saturday, 6:00 AM: one take, read like a film strip

Dev log entry for Saturday November 14, 2026, at six in the morning. Every picture marked "from the game" is a real take played overnight.

At midnight the camera in our castle set was looking at the back of a wall. This is the same set six hours later, one frame for each line of an eight-line scene, in order:

The speaker is in the picture in all eight frames, with a face you can read in seven. No walls. One back of a head. We have been keeping that count all night, because "it looks better" is not a measurement:

  • 2 AM, three sets: no speaker's face in any frame, and the camera on the wrong actor five times in nine.
  • 4 AM, the castle: speaker in frame four times in eight, a bare wall once.
  • 5 AM: six in eight.
  • 6 AM: eight in eight.

Three things got it there, and none of them was clever. The standing spots the cameras could not see were found by measuring every one of them and moved a few steps. The camera was stopped from cutting away to the listener more than twice a take. And the actors now turn slightly toward the audience when they talk to each other, as stage actors always have.

The same playing turned up a mistake that had been in front of us for hours: the character cast as the ghoul had been walking around in someone else's costume, a hooded figure in red and black. The casting was fine; one entry in her costume record pointed at the wrong character. She is herself again in the strip above.

The space station was played for the first time tonight too. Its windows look onto a field of stars, and when the scene turns dangerous the whole bridge goes red for eight seconds.

What still is not right as the sun comes up: a second show in the same sitting does not start by itself, one actor wandered off the set mid-scene, and nobody has yet played a full show with a controller in their hands. Today is for those, and for the people who make this game to wake up and play it.

The team pushed 80 project updates across Verse gameplay code, art, props and materials, audio.

items.title: Jam update: Sat 3:17 AM
items.content_html:
Jam update: Sat 3:17 AM

Saturday, November 14, 2026 at 3:17 AM Central

Saturday, 3:00 AM: the camera learns to look at the person talking

Dev log entry for Saturday November 14, 2026, written at three in the morning. Pictures marked "from the game" are real takes played tonight.

Two hours ago we opened every set like a stage so the cameras could see in. Then we did the only thing that proves anything: we played it, set after set, and wrote down what each frame actually showed.

The first pass was humbling. Four sets, sixteen lines of dialogue, and a simple count: a blank wall in the picture, zero times. That was the fix working. The speaker's face in the picture: also zero times. The camera no longer hid behind walls, but it was framing chests and elbows, and five times out of nine it was pointed at the actor who was listening.

So the camera got three new rules before the next pass. Show the one who is speaking. Aim at the face, not the middle of the body. And never choose a shot you have not checked. We played the same three sets again with the same cast.

The second count: wrong actor, none. Shots with nothing usable in them, none, where there had been nine. One true close-up of a speaking face, one two-shot worth keeping. That is not finished. Heads still get cut off when the camera lands beside an actor, and the western town's wide shot makes its cast look like ants. But it is the first time tonight the game looked like someone was directing it.

Horror turned out to have its own problem: darkness. Measured from the frames, a horror scene was about a seventh as bright as a daylight one. We did not want to wash the mood out, so the rule we settled on has two halves: a wide shot must always be bright enough to read, and a close-up may stay as dark as it likes so long as a face or a pair of eyes comes through. Each actor now carries a stronger light in dark scenes, and a follow spot finds whoever is speaking.

The other thing seen in the game for the first time tonight is the end of a take. It used to stop on a plain cut screen. Now the curtain comes down on a sheet that says "That's a wrap": what the take made at the box office, what the cast, the location and the film cost, how many stars it earned, a one-line tip, and your director level.

That sheet also taught us the night's most useful lesson. It trapped our tester: no click and no key would close it. The cause was a single unticked setting that says whether a panel is allowed to take focus. With it off, every instruction to focus the panel was ignored without a word of complaint. The same setting explains why nothing had ever answered a controller. It is ticked now, and written into our rules.

Elsewhere tonight: the director's office, where every show starts, went from a concrete yard to a room with posters, trophies and a film camera; the count of hand props we have modelled reached seventy-one, each with its own icon; and the space station got a red alert.

Still not done at three o'clock: nobody has seen a prop in an actor's hand, wide shots at night are too dark, and no one has yet played a full show with a controller. Those are next.

items.title: Jam update: Sat 1:29 AM
items.content_html:
Jam update: Sat 1:29 AM

Saturday, November 14, 2026 at 1:29 AM Central

Saturday, 1:30 AM: the night we opened every set

Dev log entry for Saturday November 14, 2026. Written overnight. Pictures are from the editor unless a caption says they are from the game.

The last thing we were told before the studio went to sleep was blunt: most of the time you cannot see the show. The camera sits behind a wall, or looks at the back of a prop, while two AI actors perform a scene nobody can watch. For a game about directing a show, that is the one fault that cannot ship.

So tonight we stopped fixing blocked shots one playtest at a time and measured all of them. A script stands a figure on every spot an actor can use, on every set, and from each spot tries every camera position the game is able to choose: the wide shot, close-ups, over-the-shoulder, pans, dollies, the crane. For each one it asks a simple question: is anything between the lens and this actor's face?

The first numbers were hard to read. In the castle, 30 camera lines in 100 reached an actor. In the old theatre, 40. In the jungle temple, 48. The widest shot, the one meant to show the whole scene, was blocked every single time on all three.

The cause turned out to be simple. Our cameras stand six to fourteen metres back, and the rooms are smaller than that. The lens was outside the building.

The fix is the oldest trick in film and television: a set is not a room, it is a stage with one wall missing. We opened every set on the side where the cameras work. Outer walls came off, a bay window and a tower roof left the castle, partitions and a vending machine left the theatre, a barn lost half its west wall. Each set also got a marker that says "the audience sits here", and no camera is allowed to stand further back than it.

By a quarter past one, all eight sets measured between 90 and 99 clear lines in 100. The game's own camera code changed too: every shot now checks that it can see its actor before it is used, and picks a different shot if it cannot.

Then we played it, and the game reminded us that a measurement is not a show. In the first take on the western town, every shot was rejected and replaced, because one actor was sitting in a chair that no camera could see, and our new rule insisted on seeing everyone. The picture below is from the build before tonight's changes, and it is exactly the complaint we started with: the director's panel is up, and behind it the camera is staring at a porch rail.

That chair has been moved and the rule corrected. The same shot gets taken again on the next build, and we will post it either way.

Other things that moved tonight:

  • Money. A take now costs something: rent for the location, film for every take, and the cast's day rates. It earns box office, a score in stars, and progress toward the next director level. The first take played on the new rules made $420, cost $350, and earned one star with the advice "more emotions".
  • Props. Forty-five hand props of our own are modelled, with twenty-four new short animations for holding and using them. No actor has held one in the game yet; that test is running as this is written.
  • The game played itself, almost. For the first time one of our AI helpers drove the whole game by mouse, from the title screen through casting, the set, the genre and a full eight-line take to the final CUT, and then filed a list of everything that was wrong with the menus on the way.

What is honest to say at half past one: the sets are open, the numbers are good, the code is in, and none of it has yet been watched working in a full take with the actors in every frame. That is what the rest of the night is for.

We're deep into the weekend with about 42 hours still on the clock, and the team has been busy with 87 updates across gameplay code, art, props, materials, and audio. Right now we're doing a big sight-line audit, checking every camera position against every set and then opening things up by pulling out walls and reworking layouts so the action is easy to see. No big milestones to announce just yet, but plenty of polish is landing behind the scenes. Stay tuned for visuals soon!

In progress

  • Sight-line audit: trace every camera position against every set, then open the sets (walls out, layouts changed)

items.title: MegaJam26 begins
items.content_html:
MegaJam26 begins

Thursday, November 12, 2026 at 9:35 AM Central

MegaJam26 is underway. Over the next few days our studio is building a brand-new Fortnite island in UEFN for the GlassDoor MegaJam26 benefit jam, and this devlog follows along from the first blank level to the final build. The jam runs until Sunday, November 15 at 7:59 PM Central. Today was all about getting set up: the team is in place, roles are assigned, the project and our task board are ready, and the first gameplay goals are on the list. Our studio team works alongside AI-assisted production tools, and this log itself is assembled automatically every few hours from our progress, then checked before it goes out. Check back for screenshots, clips and new features as the island comes together.
